title: From Requirements to Architecture: Functional, Non-Functional, and the Well-Architected Framework
bodyMarkdown:
## Why requirements drive every decision

Design and planning is the largest exam domain (about 25% of the blueprint), and nearly every question in it reduces to one skill: read a scenario, separate what is *required* from what is merely *mentioned*, and pick the cheapest architecture that satisfies the required parts. Before you pick a service, you classify and quantify the requirements. Most wrong answers on the exam are not wrong technology; they are right technology applied at the wrong level of resilience, scale or cost.

### Functional, non-functional and business requirements

| Type | Answers | Examples | Drives |
|------|---------|----------|--------|
| **Functional (FR)** | *What* the system does | "A user can place an order", "Export a monthly report" | Features, APIs, data model |
| **Non-functional (NFR)** | *How well* it does it | p99 latency under 300 ms, survive a zone outage, EU data residency | Compute, storage and network choices, SLOs |
| **Business** | *Why* it exists | Cut TCO 20%, reduce churn, launch in 3 new countries | KPIs, ROI, prioritization, build/buy decisions |
| **Constraint** | What you cannot change | Budget cap, existing licenses, a hard cutover date, regulation | Which options are even eligible |

Exam trap: latency, throughput, availability, durability, residency, security and recoverability statements are all **non-functional**, even when the stakeholder phrases them as features ("the checkout must stay up if a zone fails"). A statement is functional only if it describes a capability a user can invoke.

Business requirements are often hidden in the narrative: "the CFO wants to avoid upfront capital spend" points to consumption-based services; "the team has no Kubernetes experience" points away from GKE Standard; "the launch is in eight weeks" points to rehost or SaaS rather than refactor. Treat these as hard inputs, not color.

## Turning NFRs into measurable targets

A vague NFR cannot be designed against or tested. Convert each one into an indicator, an objective and a window.

- **SLI (service level indicator)**: the measurement, for example the fraction of checkout requests that return successfully in under 300 ms.
- **SLO (service level objective)**: a target for the SLI over a period. Cloud Monitoring's [service monitoring concepts](https://cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring) describe an SLO as a target value for an SLI measured over a period of time, normally set below 100%, and compliance periods can be calendar-based (weekly, monthly) or a rolling window of 1 to 30 days.
- **Error budget**: the tolerated failure, computed as (1 - SLO goal) x eligible events in the compliance period. When the budget is spent, the SLO is violated, and that is the signal to pause risky releases and invest in reliability.
- **SLA**: the contractual promise to customers, with remedies. Internal SLOs are normally tighter than the SLA so you notice trouble before you owe credits.

The Well-Architected [reliability pillar](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/reliability) begins with two principles that map directly to exam questions: *define reliability based on user-experience goals* and *set realistic targets for reliability*. Measure what users see (request success ratio, latency) rather than only server-centric metrics such as CPU.

### What availability numbers mean in minutes

Memorize the order of magnitude over a 30-day month (43,200 minutes):

| Availability target | Allowed downtime per 30 days |
|---------------------|------------------------------|
| 99% | about 7.2 hours |
| 99.9% | about 43 minutes |
| 99.95% | about 21.6 minutes |
| 99.99% | about 4.3 minutes |
| 99.999% | about 26 seconds |

Two consequences matter in design. First, a 99.99% target cannot be met with a runbook that needs a human to wake up and act, so it forces automated failover. Second, availability of components in series multiplies: two hard dependencies at 99.9% each give roughly 99.8% for the chain, so the composite can never beat its weakest serial link. Stating the target as a number is what lets you decide whether a regional deployment is enough or a multi-region design is justified.

## The Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework

Use the [Well-Architected Framework](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework) as a review checklist. It currently has **six pillars**:

| Pillar | Focus |
|--------|-------|
| **Operational excellence** | Efficiently deploy, operate, monitor and manage workloads (CI/CD, observability, automation) |
| **Security, privacy and compliance** | Protect data and workloads, design for privacy, meet regulatory requirements |
| **Reliability** | Resilient, highly available workloads that meet recovery targets |
| **Cost optimization** | Maximize the business value of your Google Cloud investment |
| **Performance optimization** | Design and tune resources for the performance the workload needs |
| **Sustainability** | Build and manage environmentally sustainable workloads |

On top of the pillars the framework publishes cross-pillar *perspectives* for **AI and ML** and for **financial services**. Older study material lists five pillars; sustainability is now a pillar of its own, so do not eliminate an answer just because it cites it.

The framework's [system design principles](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/system-design) are the recurring "why" behind answer choices: design for change, document the architecture and its decision rationale, simplify and use managed services, decouple components, and prefer stateless designs because they scale quickly and tolerate hard restarts. When two options both meet the requirements, these principles break the tie: the simpler, more managed, more decoupled one wins.

Pillars pull against each other, and the exam tests whether you notice. Maximum redundancy is a reliability win and a cost loss; aggressive caching is a performance win and a consistency risk; locking down every API is a security win and an operational-excellence cost. The correct answer is rarely "maximize one pillar"; it is "meet the stated requirement and no more".

The [cost optimization pillar](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/cost-optimization) states this directly: align cloud spending with business value, build cost awareness, provision only what you need and pay only for what you consume, and optimize continuously.

## Requirements elicitation checklist

1. Capture FRs as user stories and NFRs as numbers with time windows ("99.95% monthly", "p95 under 500 ms", "RPO 5 minutes").
2. List constraints: budget, regulation, residency, existing licenses, team skills, deadlines, and systems that cannot change.
3. Tier workloads by criticality (tier 1 revenue-critical, tier 3 tolerant). HA and DR spend is allocated per tier, not per company.
4. Define KPIs and the ROI model before the project so success is verifiable (Module 5 covers this).
5. Record trade-offs and rejected options explicitly. Documenting rationale is itself a framework principle.
6. Check the result against each pillar and note which pillar you consciously traded away.

## Gemini Cloud Assist in design reviews

[Gemini Cloud Assist](https://cloud.google.com/gemini/docs/cloud-assist/overview) is the AI assistance built into Google Cloud. Its documented capabilities include designing and configuring architectures from natural language, generating infrastructure-as-code (Terraform, gcloud, kubectl), selecting IAM roles, running AI-driven investigations over logs to find root causes, and analyzing cost anomalies and spending in natural language. It is reachable from the Cloud Assist panel in the console, Application Design Center, Database Center and investigations from the console, CLI and IDEs. Treat it as an accelerator for analysis grounded in your environment. It does not decide your requirements, and an exam scenario that asks "which tool helps investigate a cost spike or troubleshoot a misconfiguration in the console using natural language" is pointing at it, not at Model Garden, Model Armor or AI Hypercomputer.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Starting from a product.** "We use GKE, so..." before any NFR is written. Requirements first, services second.
- **Gold-plating resilience.** Multi-region active-active for an internal tool used by 20 people during business hours. The cost pillar exists to challenge exactly this.
- **Unmeasurable goals.** "Fast", "highly available", "better performance". Without a number and a window you cannot choose between a zonal and a regional design, or know when you have succeeded.
- **Designing to the SLA instead of the SLO.** The contractual number is the floor you must never breach, not the target you engineer toward.
- **Ignoring the composite.** Quoting 99.99% for one component while the user path crosses four serial dependencies.
- **Treating the framework as a one-time gate.** Reviews should recur as the design changes; the framework's own principle is to design for change.
- **Missing hidden constraints.** Data residency, existing licenses and team skills are usually in a single sentence of the scenario and often eliminate half the options.
- **Over-trusting the assistant.** An AI recommendation without a requirement behind it is still a guess.

## Exam tips

- **Classify by quality attribute.** Latency, availability, durability, residency and security statements are non-functional even when worded as features; only user-invocable capabilities are functional.
- **Right-size resilience.** If a scenario describes a low-value or internal workload and an option maximizes redundancy, the cost optimization pillar makes that option wrong.
- **Strong KPIs and SLOs have a number, a baseline and a window.** "p95 latency from 1,200 ms to under 500 ms within 90 days" beats any qualitative phrasing.
- **Remember six pillars.** Operational excellence, security/privacy/compliance, reliability, cost optimization, performance optimization and sustainability.
- **SLO is the internal target, SLA the contractual one.** Error budget is (1 - SLO) of eligible events in the compliance period.
- **Tie-breaker principle.** When two designs both meet the requirements, choose the simpler, more managed, more decoupled and stateless one.
- **Gemini Cloud Assist is the console and CLI assistant** for design help, cost investigation and troubleshooting; Model Garden is a model catalog, Model Armor screens prompts and responses, AI Hypercomputer is AI infrastructure.
- **Read constraints as eliminators.** Budget caps, deadlines, residency and team skills are first-class requirements and usually disqualify at least two options.
